Pop: Pop is built around hooks, big choruses, and polish — music designed to be immediately catchy and radio-ready. Expect strong melodies, tight production, and songs that reward repeat listens.
Rap/Hip Hop: Hip hop centers rhythm, wordplay, and voice — built on beats, samples, and flow. It spans party anthems, introspective storytelling, and boundary-pushing production.
Rock: Rock is guitar-and-rhythm-section music with roots in blues and folk, ranging from raw garage energy to arena-sized anthems. Look for riffs, live-band energy, and decades of subgenres to dig into.
Alternative: Alternative grew out of underground and college-radio scenes as a counterpoint to mainstream rock and pop. It covers a lot of ground — jangly guitars, noisy experimentation, moody atmosphere — united by a DIY, non-mainstream spirit.
Electro: Electronic music built from synthesizers, drum machines, and studio production rather than traditional instruments. Ranges from dancefloor-focused tracks to ambient, textural listening.
Dance: Dance music is made for movement — four-on-the-floor beats, build-ups, and drops engineered for clubs and festivals. House, techno, and EDM all live here.
R&B: R&B blends soulful vocals with smooth, groove-driven production. Expect emotive singing, rich harmonies, and a strong pocket between rhythm and melody.
Jazz: Jazz is built on improvisation, swing, and complex harmony, with roots in blues and ragtime. Every listen can sound different — the same tune reinterpreted in real time.
Classical: Classical spans centuries of orchestral, chamber, and solo instrumental composition. Expect structured forms, dynamic range, and music written to be studied as much as felt.
Reggae/Dancehall: Reggae grew out of Jamaica in the late 1960s, built around off-beat guitar skanks, deep basslines, and a laid-back groove. Dancehall picked up the tempo and the electronic production in the decades after.
Country: Country tells stories — about home, heartbreak, and everyday life — over guitar, steel, and fiddle-driven arrangements rooted in American folk and blues traditions.
Metal: Metal pushes rock's intensity further with heavier riffs, faster tempos, and more aggressive vocals and drumming. It splits into dozens of subgenres, from doom's slow crush to thrash's speed.
Blues: Blues is the foundation a lot of modern popular music is built on — twelve-bar structures, call-and-response phrasing, and raw emotional delivery, often centered on guitar and voice.
Latin: Latin covers an enormous range of styles from across Latin America and Spain — salsa, reggaeton, bachata, and more — united by rhythm-forward arrangements and strong dance traditions.
Films/Games: Music written for screen and interactive media — scores and soundtracks built to support a story, mood, or setting rather than stand alone as singles.
Kids: Music made for younger listeners — simple, upbeat, and often tied to shows, movies, or sing-along formats.
Comedy: Comedy music uses song as a vehicle for humor — parody, novelty tracks, and songs built around a joke or bit as much as a melody.
Soul & Funk: Soul and funk emphasize groove, rhythm section interplay, and expressive vocal performance — music built to move both your body and your emotions.
World: A broad catch-all for music rooted in traditions from outside the Western pop mainstream — wide-ranging in instrumentation, language, and style.
Indie: Independently produced or independently minded music that sits outside major-label pop conventions — often lower-fi, more personal, and stylistically restless.
Rap: Hip hop centers rhythm, wordplay, and voice — built on beats, samples, and flow. It spans party anthems, introspective storytelling, and boundary-pushing production.
Reggae: Reggae grew out of Jamaica in the late 1960s, built around off-beat guitar skanks, deep basslines, and a laid-back groove.
Electronic: Electronic music built from synthesizers, drum machines, and studio production rather than traditional instruments. Ranges from dancefloor-focused tracks to ambient, textural listening.
Dance & EDM: Dance music is made for movement — four-on-the-floor beats, build-ups, and drops engineered for clubs and festivals. House, techno, and EDM all live here.
Latin music: Latin covers an enormous range of styles from across Latin America and Spain — salsa, reggaeton, bachata, and more — united by rhythm-forward arrangements and strong dance traditions.
Soundtracks: Music written for screen and interactive media — scores and soundtracks built to support a story, mood, or setting rather than stand alone as singles.
K-pop: South Korea's pop industry, known for tightly produced, genre-blending songs paired with elaborate choreography and a strong visual identity — often built around idol groups.
Folk & singer-songwriter: Music centered on voice, acoustic instrumentation, and personal or narrative songwriting, with roots in traditional folk music passed down and reinterpreted over generations.
African music: A vast range of traditions and modern styles from across the African continent — from Afrobeats and highlife to traditional percussion-driven and vocal music.
Asian music: A broad catch-all spanning pop, traditional, and folk styles from across Asia, reflecting a huge range of languages, instrumentation, and regional traditions.
Brazilian music: Brazil's enormously varied musical tradition — samba, bossa nova, MPB, and more — known for intricate rhythm, warmth, and strong melodic sensibility.
